title: Dispatch: three families of meaningful or rule-built text fail where a learned glyph chain succeeds, and for the same reason
statement: Three open questions were measured on the practice split this hour, each with the manuscript's token layout. Sound-collapsing encodings of Latin, Italian and German reach the manuscript's conditional glyph entropy (1.94 bits) only by cutting the alphabet to nine or ten symbols and the single-glyph entropy to about 2.4 bits, while the manuscript keeps 3.9 bits and ties 79% of glyph occurrences to one word position (Latin 66%) (K-014-open-1). A hand-written slot grammar with grammatical one-glyph edits and whole-word reuse matches the entropy and the near-copies without learning any transition table, but not the singletons (0.62 against 0.71) or the within-page reuse (0.20 against 0.31), and the gap grows with text size (K-008-open-1). Latin, Esperanto and a priori root-and-modifier codes of Latin give almost none of the cross-word edge dependence (shuffle-corrected 0.00 to 0.06 against 0.18), while R-017's learned chain gives most of it (K-001-open-2). The common thread: the manuscript is predictable because its glyphs are bound to positions inside the word and across the word space, a property of how the text was written down, which a chain learned from the pages copies and no lexicon or grammar tried here produces. Esperanto now has two pinned texts and enters reference comparisons. Next: the invented-language test should start from a writing rule that binds word ends to the next word's start, not from a lexicon; the scribe fact (P-G-009) at alpha 0.01; and the book-form attack cut once reviewed.
